blocks.title: Gravitational wave
blocks.text: A gravitational wave is a stretching and compressing of space and can be observed by measuring the change in length between two objects. Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of spacetime, produced by violent cosmic events like colliding black holes or neutron stars, that travel at the speed of light, carrying information about their source.

The simplest example to understand gravitational waves: if we throw a stone into a pond, the stone creates ripples on the water surface (spacetime). These ripples travel outward, carrying information about the stone (the cosmic event). They can be detected on the shore (by gravitational wave observatories), revealing the stone's presence and properties.

Gravitational waves are a prediction of Einstein's theory of general relativity which is confirmed by observations and is opening a new window into the universe's most extreme phenomena. According to Einstein's general theory of relativity, gravity is not a force but a curvature of spacetime caused by massive bodies. Gravity is like a dent in a mattress: heavy things warp (printed 'wrap') the space around them, and that is why we feel gravity. Albert Einstein (1879-1955), a German-born theoretical physicist, is one of the world's most renowned and influential scientists.

Gravitational waves, as initially predicted by Albert Einstein in 1916, are ripples in spacetime that were first detected in 2015. The print describes that first observation as waves produced from two colliding neutron stars; topic 8.7 of the same book states that the waves recorded on 14 September 2015 came from a collision between two black holes, which is the accepted account. In such a merging system there is a gradual increase in the frequency and amplitude of the waves.

blocks.title: Binary system
blocks.text: A binary system (BS), in the context of gravitational waves, is a system consisting of two compact objects, such as black holes, neutron stars or white dwarfs, which are orbiting each other and emitting gravitational waves.
Four basic types of gravitational waves

items: Continuous GWs: when a single massive object spins at a constant rate, such as a neutron star, continuous GWs are produced with the same frequency and amplitude. White dwarf binary systems produce continuous GWs.
Compact binary inspiral GWs (printed 'inspirational'): produced when a binary system, such as binary neutron stars, binary black holes, or a neutron star and a black hole, orbit each other.
Burst GWs: produced by violent events like supernovae, gamma-ray bursts or cosmic strings.
Stochastic GWs: weak, random signals produced by the superposition of many weak gravitational wave sources, such as distant binary systems. These GWs are the most difficult to detect.

blocks.text: Every physical object that accelerates produces gravitational waves, including vehicles and aeroplanes; but the masses and accelerations of objects on the Earth are too small to make gravitational waves big enough to be detected with our instruments. Dr. Nergis Mavalvala, a Pakistani-American astrophysicist at MIT, is known for her work on gravitational waves.

As binary systems (also termed binaries) orbit each other they emit gravitational waves, which can be detected by observatories like LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory) in the USA and Virgo, a large-scale gravitational wave observatory in Cascina, Italy. The waves carry information about the system's mass, spin and merger dynamics, offering insights into these extreme cosmic objects, and move with the speed of light. Binary systems are significant sources of gravitational waves, and their mergers (the collision and union of two massive objects resulting in a more massive single object) are among the most intense cosmic events.

As the masses orbit and accelerate, their gravitational intensity fluctuates, generating waves that radiate outward in all directions, like a series of concentric spheres with the binary system at the centre. These waves are not bound by the binary system's gravity; instead they travel freely through spacetime at the speed of light, weakening in intensity as they move away from the source. The characteristics of GWs depend on the system's properties, such as the masses of the objects, the orbital period and frequency, and the eccentricity of the orbit, a measure of the amount by which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.

Gravitational waves passing through a body with mass can cause the body to experience periodic stretching and compressing, also known as spacetime distortion. This effect is known as tidal forces and is a result of the gravitational wave's oscillating nature. As the wave passes through the body, it causes the spacetime around the body to oscillate, leading to a periodic stretching and compressing of the body in the direction perpendicular to the wave's propagation. This effect is similar to how the tides on the Earth are caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun. The amount of stretching and compressing depends on the strength of the wave and on the mass and size of the body; this effect is an important prediction of Einstein's theory of general relativity.

Gravitational waves generated by far-off celestial events, such as the merger of two black holes or neutron stars, pass through the Earth. However, the amplitude of these waves is extremely small, typically of the order of 10^-21 to 10^-22 metres, so the distortion is incredibly tiny and requires extremely sensitive instruments to detect. Despite their small amplitude, gravitational waves offer a unique window into the universe, allowing us to study strong-field gravity, test general relativity, and explore the universe in ways previously impossible.

blocks.caption: Gravitational waves and the laser interferometer (original diagram after Figure 8.9 and topics 8.6 and 8.7).
blocks.long_description: Two compact objects such as black holes or neutron stars orbiting each other disturb spacetime, and the disturbance spreads outward at the speed of light as gravitational waves. A passing wave stretches space in one direction while squeezing it in the perpendicular one, then the reverse, so a ring of free masses becomes alternately a wide and a tall ellipse; at the Earth the change is only about 10^-21 to 10^-22 metres. A laser interferometer detects this by splitting a laser beam into two long perpendicular arms, bouncing the beams between mirrors and recombining them: a change in the arm lengths alters the phase between the beams and so the interference pattern at the photodetector.

blocks.prompt: What are gravitational waves, who predicted them, and how are tidal forces formed (MCQ 8.10, 8.11, 8.13; constructed response 8.6)?
blocks.explanation: Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of spacetime, predicted by Albert Einstein in 1916 from general relativity and produced mainly by accelerating massive bodies such as a binary black hole merger. As a wave passes through a body it makes the spacetime around it oscillate, so the body is periodically stretched and compressed perpendicular to the wave's direction; these periodic stretching and squeezing effects are the tidal forces, similar to the tides raised on the Earth by the Moon and the Sun.

items: Gravitational waves: ripples in spacetime from violent cosmic events, travelling at the speed of light; predicted by Einstein (1916), first detected in 2015. Gravity is a curvature of spacetime (a dent in a mattress).

Binary system: two compact objects orbiting and radiating. Types: continuous, compact binary inspiral, burst, stochastic. Depend on masses, orbital period and frequency, eccentricity. Tidal forces: periodic stretching and squeezing; amplitude 10^-21 to 10^-22 m at the Earth.
